strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 8 diverse benchmarks (2D visual grounding, 3D spatial reasoning, navigation) with state-of-the-art results on 7/8 tasks
Real-world robot deployment demonstrating practical feasibility and generalization beyond simulation
Addresses two genuine problems in embodied AI: geometric adaptability gap (2D training vs 3D reasoning) and embodiment constraint gap (physical feasibility)
Large-scale integrated training dataset with 5.2M samples from diverse sources (general reasoning, visual grounding, 3D understanding, spatial reasoning, active exploration)
Multimodal flexibility: handles diverse input modalities (RGB, RGB-D, video) and output formats (2D/3D coordinates, natural language)
Thoughtful two-stage training strategy (supervised finetuning followed by TE-GRFO refinement with progressive curriculum learning)
Clear ablation studies showing the effectiveness of individual components (TAGR module, embodiment-aware training)
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: TAGR is a straightforward learned gating mechanism using established Gumbel-Softmax techniques; embodiment-aware training combines existing GRFO framework with standard multi-task and curriculum learning

Unclear contribution attribution: impossible to determine whether improvements stem from architectural innovations, training strategy, or dataset engineering with 5.2M samples; TAGR only improves baseline by 1.22%
Minimal real-world validation: only 2 examples of actual robot execution shown despite claiming real-world deployment as a key contribution
Coarse-grained evaluation metrics: success rates are binary; missing systematic error analysis, failure mode characterization, and performance on different task categories
Physical constraint enforcement unclear: constraints appear to be encouraged through learned rewards rather than actually enforced; no constraint violation rate metrics provided

Superficial task-adaptivity analysis: Figure 4 shows word activation frequencies but lacks quantitative precision/recall analysis; only 4 case studies presented; no analysis of when gating decisions fail
Missing contribution isolation: no ablation separating dataset composition impact from architectural contribution despite 5.2M training samples likely being the dominant factor
No computational efficiency analysis: inference time, training time, and memory requirements not discussed, which is critical for practical embodied deployment
Limited generalization testing: no evaluation on novel robot morphologies, completely new environments, or alternative sensor modalities despite claiming versatility
Reproducibility concerns: multi-stage training with numerous hyperparameters and no code release mentioned; many design choices (KL regularization, curriculum schedule) lack ablation justification

strengths: Addresses well-motivated and important problems in embodied AI (geometric adaptability gap and embodiment constraint gap) with clear practical relevance
Strong empirical results achieving state-of-the-art on 7 out of 8 benchmarks with significant improvements on 3D tasks (e.g., +2.3 to +8.5 on 3D benchmarks) and ObjNav (+5.4 SPL)

Comprehensive and rigorous experimental evaluation spanning 8 public benchmarks, 4 in-house primitive benchmarks, in-simulator end-to-end evaluation, and real-world robot deployment - unusually thorough coverage

Effective qualitative analysis demonstrating model behavior: Figure 4 shows interpretable gate activation patterns, Figure 5 demonstrates linguistic sensitivity, Figure 7 illustrates embodiment-aware reasoning with detailed considerations
Well-designed two-stage training paradigm combining omnisupervised finetuning with embodiment-aware reinforced finetuning that jointly optimizes task correctness and physical feasibility
Thorough documentation with detailed appendices including implementation specifics, dataset compositions, hyperparameter configurations, and extensive qualitative examples supporting reproducibility
Real-world robot validation (Appendix F) strengthens claims beyond simulation and demonstrates practical applicability of the approach
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Task-Adaptive Gated Router uses straightforward temperature-scaled softmax gating (a standard technique), and embodiment-aware training combines existing methods (RL finetuning, curriculum learning) in conventional ways

Insufficient analysis of the gating mechanism: Figure 4 shows which words activate gates but lacks depth in explaining why specific semantic concepts require 3D reasoning; missing systematic categorization of tasks by 3D requirements and analysis of failure modes

Embodiment-aware training lacks component-level ablation: TE-GRFO involves multiple elements (r^task, r^embed, curriculum scheduling, KL regularization) but no ablations on individual components; design choices (e.g., KL divergence necessity, λ_t sensitivity) are not well justified
Missing computational cost analysis: No runtime comparisons, inference time overhead, or memory requirements provided - critical for real-world embodied agent deployment

Limited quantitative validation of embodiment constraints: Real-world experiments (Figures 10-11) are qualitative demonstrations only; lack quantitative metrics on kinematic feasibility, collision avoidance, and physical plan validity

Dataset composition and generalization concerns: 5.2M training samples mentioned but task distribution unclear; potential dataset imbalance; limited cross-dataset generalization analysis despite using multiple diverse benchmarks

Incomplete error and failure analysis: No systematic investigation of when/why OmniEVA fails; missing analysis of performance on edge cases or when 3D information is unavailable; no analysis of failure modes beyond brief examples

Presentation clarity issues: Dense technical content makes the paper difficult to follow; main contributions not sufficiently prominent; some notation inconsistencies; relationship between training stages could be explained more clearly
Limited real-world validation scope: Only two qualitative robot scenarios shown; would benefit from systematic evaluation of multiple tasks and quantitative feasibility metrics on real hardware

Reproducibility concerns: No mention of code release; partial use of in-house datasets limits reproducibility; some TE-GRFO implementation details could be clearer; computational resources and training procedures not fully specified
